questions.stem_markdown: A parent of a 15-year-old says, "He used to want to do everything with us, but now he is focused on friends, has started a first romantic relationship, and seems to be trying out different social roles." Which explanation best matches the developmental tasks described in the notes?

options.text: This mainly reflects physical/biological development through puberty and body image change
This mainly reflects cognitive development through abstract thinking, problem-solving, and future planning
This mainly reflects emotional development through identity formation, independence, and managing emotions
This mainly reflects social development through peer relationships, intimacy, separation from parents, and experimentation with roles
This mainly reflects moral/ethical development through personal values, autonomy, and responsibility

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes describe **social** development in adolescence as involving **peer relationships, intimacy or romantic relationships, separation from parents, and experimentation with roles**. That cluster matches this vignette most closely.

why_others_wrong.A: Physical and biological development in the notes refers to puberty, sexual maturation, and body image development rather than the peer and role changes described here.
why_others_wrong.B: Cognitive development is about movement from concrete to abstract thinking, plus problem-solving and future planning, which is not the main theme of this stem.
why_others_wrong.C: Emotional development includes identity formation, independence, and managing emotions, but the strongest note-based fit here is the social domain.
why_others_wrong.E: Moral and ethical development focuses on personal values, autonomy, and responsibility rather than peer intimacy and role experimentation.

key_takeaways: Social development in adolescence includes peer relationships and romantic intimacy.
Separation from parents and experimentation with roles are described as normal social developmental tasks.
Not every change in adolescent behaviour is pathological; some reflect expected development.

questions.stem_markdown: During a follow-up consultation, a 16-year-old is trying to balance school, sport, casual work, and future study plans. Which consultation approach best uses the cognitive developmental changes described in the notes?

options.text: Direct almost all discussion to the parents because adolescents are not yet ready for abstract reasoning
Keep the discussion concrete only and avoid asking about future consequences or alternative options
Ask the young person to weigh several options, think ahead, and help problem-solve the next steps
Avoid involving the young person in planning until adulthood because future planning is not part of adolescent development
Focus only on current emotions because multidimensional thinking is not expected until after adolescence

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes describe adolescent **cognitive** development as moving from **concrete to abstract thinking** and developing **problem-solving** and **future planning**. The stage table also notes that middle adolescence becomes capable of **planned, abstract, multidimensional thought**, so option C best fits a developmentally appropriate approach.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes do not support excluding the adolescent from reasoning and planning; instead, they describe growing cognitive capacity during adolescence.
why_others_wrong.B: Avoiding future consequences and alternative options ignores the note-based development of abstract thinking and problem-solving.
why_others_wrong.D: Future planning is explicitly listed in the notes as part of adolescent cognitive development.
why_others_wrong.E: The source material states that multidimensional and abstract thinking develop during adolescence rather than only after it.

key_takeaways: Adolescent cognitive development includes abstract thinking, problem-solving, and future planning.
Middle adolescence is associated with more planned and multidimensional thought.
Consultation style should increasingly involve the young person in reasoning through options.
